::: {.callout-important}
## Complete this before the workshop

This setup takes most people between thirty minutes and two hours, and some of
it cannot be hurried: package installation and the CmdStan build both take time
that depends on your machine and your network.

**There is no time set aside during the workshop to install or repair
software.** If you arrive without a working installation you will be able to
watch, but you will not be able to fit models alongside the demonstrations, and
most of the day is spent fitting models.

Work through this document, then run the verification check in the final
section. Do it early, so that a problem has time to be resolved before the
day.
:::

## Software required

| Software | Purpose |
|---|---|
| R | the language everything else runs in |
| A C++ toolchain | compiles each Bayesian model before it is fitted |
| CmdStan | the sampler that fits the models |
| Positron | the editor used throughout the workshop |
| Git | retrieves the workshop materials |

The C++ toolchain is the part that differs by operating system, and it is the
part that fails most often. On Windows it is Rtools, on macOS the Xcode Command
Line Tools, and on Linux the standard build tools.

Bayesian model fitting works differently from most R modelling. Each model is
translated into C++, compiled into a program, and run. That is why a compiler is
needed at all, and why the first fit of a session takes longer than later ones.

## Route by operating system

**Windows is the tested and recommended route**, and it is the one described in
most detail below. The difficulties Stan had on Windows historically came from
an older interface, `rstan`, which required matched versions of several
compiled packages. The current interface, `cmdstanr`, avoids most of that.

**Linux is also tested.** macOS is not, because the workshop organisers have no
Mac available. Mac users should follow the outline in the macOS section, which
points to the authoritative upstream instructions, and then run the same
verification check as everyone else. The check is what determines whether you
are ready, not which instructions you followed.

The Windows Subsystem for Linux is a fallback for one situation only, where
compilation on Windows is blocked by security policy on a machine you cannot
change. It is not a simpler route: it means a second installation of R, a second
package library and a different way of referring to your files. Do not start
there.

---

# Windows

## R and Rtools

Install R first, then Rtools.

Download R from [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/base/) and
install whichever version CRAN currently offers — do not go looking for an
older one. This document was written against R 4.5.x, and has since been
re-verified against R 4.6.1 (see the Linux section below); either is fine.
What matters is that Rtools matches the R you install, not which minor version
that is.

Then install the matching **Rtools**, from
[CRAN's Rtools page](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/). CRAN's
own page names it inconsistently — you may see "Rtools45", "RTools 4.5" or
"Rtools for R 4.5.x" — these all mean the same installer. Rtools version
numbers do not track R's one-for-one: **Rtools 4.5 is current for every R
version from 4.5.0 onward**, including R 4.6.x, so do not go looking for a
separate "Rtools 4.6" — there is not one as of this writing. Check CRAN's
Rtools page for the current mapping, since this changes as new R and Rtools
versions are released. Accept the default installation location.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Rtools must match your version of R

An Rtools built for an earlier R than the one you installed is the most common
single cause of setup failure, and the error it produces does not mention
version numbers. Check CRAN's Rtools page for which Rtools release currently
covers your R version — do not assume the two version numbers must match
exactly, since one Rtools release can cover several R releases.
:::

## Positron

Download and install [Positron](https://positron.posit.co/). It will find your R
installation automatically. If you installed R after Positron, restart Positron
so that it detects it.

## Git

Install [Git for Windows](https://git-scm.com/download/win), accepting the
defaults. Git is used to retrieve the workshop materials, as described in
the workshop materials section below.

## R packages

Open Positron and run the following in the R console.

`cmdstanr` is not on CRAN, so it comes from the Stan project's own repository:

```r
install.packages("cmdstanr",
                 repos = c("https://stan-dev.r-universe.dev",
                           getOption("repos")))
```

Then the rest:

```r
install.packages(c("brms", "posterior", "bayesplot",
                   "ggplot2", "dplyr", "tidyr", "drc"))
```

::: {.callout-note}
## rstan is a dependency, not a step

`brms` installs `rstan` as a dependency. That is expected: `rstan` must be
installed, but the workshop does not use it as the sampler, so it does not
matter if you never call it directly. No further action is needed here — the
next step is `bayesnec`, below.
:::

`bayesnec` is installed from the development branch, which contains changes not
yet released to CRAN and is what the course material is built against. This
needs the `remotes` package first — install it if you have not already:

```r
install.packages("remotes")
```

Then install `bayesnec` itself:

```r
remotes::install_github("open-AIMS/bayesnec", ref = "dev")
```

If you paste this last command in *before* installing `remotes`, R replies
that it could not find the function `install_github` (or that there is no
package called `remotes`). That is not a sign anything is broken — install
`remotes` with the command above and then re-run this one.

::: {.callout-note}
## Estimates may differ slightly from the course pages

`dev` changes as the package is developed, so a fit made now will not always
reproduce the numbers printed on the course pages to the last decimal place.
Estimates should agree to well within the width of their credible intervals. A
difference larger than that is worth raising rather than accepting.
:::

## CmdStan

First confirm the compiler is configured. On a current Rtools this passes
without doing anything; `fix = TRUE` repairs the problems it can rather than
only reporting them:

```r
cmdstanr::check_cmdstan_toolchain(fix = TRUE)
```

Then install CmdStan. Three things need setting, and all three have been
observed to stop a fresh installation:

```r
dir.create("C:/cmdstan")           # cmdstanr will not create it
options(timeout = 1800)            # the default of 60 seconds is far too short
cmdstanr::install_cmdstan(dir = "C:/cmdstan")
```

**The directory must exist first.** `install_cmdstan()` does not create it, and
stops with `Assertion on 'dir' failed: Directory 'C:/cmdstan' does not exist.`

**The download needs a longer timeout.** The CmdStan archive is about 49 MB, and
R's default `options(timeout)` is 60 seconds, which is not enough on any ordinary
connection. The `timeout` argument of `install_cmdstan()` does not govern the
download — the option does. Measured on a connection delivering about 500 KB/s:
the download failed with `Download of CmdStan failed with error` at the default,
and completed in 4.9 minutes at `timeout = 1800` with nothing else changed.
Conference and hotel networks are commonly slower than that, so set it.

The default location is inside your home directory. On many Windows machines,
particularly work-managed ones, that directory is synchronised by OneDrive, and
the CmdStan build fails there. The same failure occurs when the path contains a
space or a character outside the standard English alphabet, which happens when a
Windows username does. Installing to `C:/cmdstan` avoids all three, and costs
nothing if none of them applies to you.

Because that is not the default location, tell R where to find it in every
future session. Run `usethis::edit_r_profile()`, or open `.Rprofile` in your home
directory, and add the line below, replacing the version number with the one you
installed:

```r
options(cmdstanr_cmdstan_path = "C:/cmdstan/cmdstan-2.39.0")
```

Without this, every new session reports that CmdStan is not installed.

### Recurring problems on Windows

**`install_cmdstan()` fails.** Run it again with these arguments:

```r
cmdstanr::install_cmdstan(overwrite = TRUE, quiet = FALSE, dir = "C:/cmdstan")
```

This is the failure most recently observed on a fresh Windows machine, and this
is what resolved it. `overwrite = TRUE` is the part that matters. A first
attempt that fails partway through the build leaves a partly built directory
behind, and a second attempt without `overwrite` declines to replace it, which
produces an error resembling the original one. `quiet = FALSE` only prints more
of the build output, which is worth having because the default output is
truncated and does not identify which stage failed.

**A model compiles but no chains run.** `cmdstanr` reports "No chains finished
successfully", which names neither a cause nor a file. The usual reason is that
Rtools changed after CmdStan was installed. CmdStan builds its own `tbb.dll`,
linked against the toolchain that built it, so a CmdStan built under Rtools44
requires libraries that Rtools45 does not provide; the model still compiles and
then every chain exits immediately with `STATUS_DLL_NOT_FOUND`. Rebuild CmdStan:

```r
cmdstanr::install_cmdstan(overwrite = TRUE, dir = "C:/cmdstan")
```

Anyone who upgrades R and Rtools between installing CmdStan and the workshop will
meet this.

**Rtools is installed but `cmdstanr` cannot find it.** `cmdstanr` chooses which
Rtools to look for from your R version, and the mapping changed between
releases. Version 0.9.0 sends R 4.5.x to Rtools45; 0.8.0 sent every R from 4.4
onward to Rtools44. With an older `cmdstanr` and the Rtools45 this document
specifies, it searches for a toolchain you were never asked to install and
reports it missing. Install `cmdstanr` 0.9.0 or later, which is what the
r-universe repository above supplies. `check_setup.R` reports the version.

**Compiling is very slow.** Windows Defender inspects each newly compiled
program. A compile that should take under a minute can take several. Excluding
the `C:/cmdstan` directory from real-time scanning resolves it, where your
organisation's policy allows.

**Compiling is blocked entirely.** Some managed machines prevent newly compiled
programs from running at all. This is a policy decision rather than a
configuration problem and cannot be worked around from within R. Contact the
organisers before the workshop rather than attempting a fix on the day.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Time box the native route

Give the steps above about thirty minutes. If the verification check passes,
stop. If compilation fails for reasons of security policy rather than something
you can configure, no further adjustment will resolve it; contact the
organisers.
:::

# macOS

::: {.callout-warning}
## Untested route

The organisers have no Mac available and have not tested these steps. They point
to the upstream instructions, which are maintained by the projects themselves.
Run the verification check when you have finished; passing it is what matters,
not the route taken.
:::

1. Install R from [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/macosx/), choosing the
   build for your processor. Apple Silicon and Intel builds differ.
2. Install the Xcode Command Line Tools by running `xcode-select --install` in
   Terminal. Some packages also require `gfortran`; the CRAN macOS tools page
   describes the current requirement.
3. Install [Positron](https://positron.posit.co/) and
   [Git](https://git-scm.com/download/mac).
4. Install the R packages exactly as in the Windows section above.
5. Follow the
   [CmdStanR getting-started vignette](https://mc-stan.org/cmdstanr/articles/cmdstanr.html)
   for `check_cmdstan_toolchain()` and `install_cmdstan()`. The default
   installation path is not a problem on macOS, so `dir` need not be set.

---

# Linux

Install R through your distribution's package manager or from CRAN, and the
standard build tools --- `build-essential` on Debian and Ubuntu, or the
equivalent development group on other distributions. Install Positron and Git.
Then install the R packages as in the Windows section, and run
`check_cmdstan_toolchain()` followed by `install_cmdstan()`. The default path is
not a problem here either.

This route was verified on 2026-09-11 under Debian with R 4.6.1 and CmdStan
2.39.0.


---

# The workshop materials

The modules, the example data and `check_setup.R` are in a public GitHub
repository, <https://github.com/open-AIMS/cr_modelling_training>. Retrieve them
before the workshop and put the folder somewhere you can find again. Avoid a
folder that a cloud service synchronises while you work, such as OneDrive or
Dropbox, because a synchronising folder can lock files while R is reading them.

## Retrieval with Git

This is the route the Git installation above is for. Open a terminal --- the
Terminal pane in Positron, or Git Bash on Windows --- change to the folder you
want the materials in, and run:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/open-AIMS/cr_modelling_training.git
```

That creates a folder `cr_modelling_training` holding the whole course,
including `vignettes/check_setup.R`.

The material is revised up to the workshop. On the morning, run

```bash
git pull
```

from inside that folder to take the current version. Taking revisions this way
is the reason Git is on the list above; it has no other use during the day.

## Retrieval without Git

If Git did not install, or your machine does not allow you to run it, download
the materials as a ZIP file instead. Open
<https://github.com/open-AIMS/cr_modelling_training>, select the green "Code"
button, then "Download ZIP", and extract the archive. You end up with the same
folder. To take a later revision you download the ZIP again rather than running
`git pull`.

## The fitted models

The modules fit Bayesian models, and some of them take a while: on a four-core
machine module 5 takes about thirteen minutes and module 6 about sixteen. You do
not have to wait for that during the workshop. Every fit used in the material is
available as a single download of about 23 MB, and with those objects in place
each module loads its fits in seconds instead of sampling them.

Each module shows you the `bnec()` call that produced a fit, then the `save()`
that kept it, then the `load()` that reads it back. The download supplies the
saved objects, so the `load()` is what runs when you work through the page. That
is the same sequence a real analysis follows, and it is why the fitting call
stays visible rather than being hidden behind a cache.

From inside the `cr_modelling_training` folder, in R:

```r
source("vignettes/fetch_fits.R")
```

That downloads the archive, checks it arrived complete, and unpacks it into a
`vignettes/fits/` folder beside the modules. It is done once. Do it on a
connection you trust rather than on conference wifi on the morning.

The archive is revised while the material is being finished, so run `git pull`
and then the line above again if you collected the materials more than a few
days before the workshop. Re-running it replaces the saved fits in place.

::: {.callout-note}
## Copying the fits by hand

The archive is also on a USB stick on the day, and you can put the objects in
place yourself without running anything. The stick holds a `fits` folder
containing eighteen `.RData` files. Copy that whole folder into the `vignettes`
folder of your `cr_modelling_training` folder, so that the files end up at:

```
cr_modelling_training/vignettes/fits/m2_bnec_fit.RData
cr_modelling_training/vignettes/fits/m4_bnec_fit.RData
...
```

The path matters, because each module runs with `vignettes` as its working
directory and reads `fits/` relative to that. A `fits` folder placed at the top
level of `cr_modelling_training` is not found.
:::

The download is optional. Without it the material is complete and the modules
are slower. Run the `bnec()` chunk each module shows, which is the one marked as
not evaluated, followed by its `save()` line. That writes the same file into `fits/`, and the
`load()` below it then works exactly as it does for everyone else.

The verification check below reports whether the fitted models are present, so
you do not have to work it out yourself.

## Opening the materials in Positron

Use "File > Open Folder" and select the `cr_modelling_training` folder. R then
starts in that folder, so a relative path such as
`source("vignettes/check_setup.R")` resolves without you typing a full path.

---

# The verification check

`check_setup.R` is supplied alongside this document, in the `vignettes/` folder
of the materials you retrieved in the previous section. It installs nothing. It reports what you have, compiles and fits a
small model, and finishes with either READY or NOT READY.

The most reliable way to run it is to open `check_setup.R` itself in Positron
(not just this document) and run the whole file from there — for example with
Positron's "Source" button, or by selecting all the code and running it.
Positron then runs it from the folder the file is saved in, which avoids the
error below.

If you instead want to run it from the R console with `source()`, R needs to
be told where the file is. Pasting

```r
source("check_setup.R", echo = FALSE)
```

only works if your R console's *working directory* is already the
`vignettes/` folder — otherwise you will see:

```
Warning message:
In file(filename, "r", encoding = encoding) :
  cannot open file 'check_setup.R': No such file or directory
Error in `file()`:
! cannot open the connection
```

This is not a sign of a broken installation; it means R was looking in the
wrong folder. Either open `check_setup.R` in Positron and run it from there
(the first option above), or give `source()` the full path to the file, for
example:

```r
source("C:/path/to/cr_modelling_training/vignettes/check_setup.R", echo = FALSE)
```

replacing the path with wherever you saved the workshop materials.

Every run takes a few minutes, because it compiles a model each time rather than
reusing an earlier build. That is deliberate: reusing a build would let the check
pass without ever invoking the compiler, which is the thing being tested.

A successful run ends like this:

```
Summary
-------
READY. Every check passed.
```

A warning rather than a failure means you can follow the workshop but something
is not as expected --- a home directory the CmdStan build cannot use, or a
`cmdstanr` too old for the Rtools these instructions specify. Read the warning
and act on it if you can.
